summary: Specifies the conventions for using the Advanced Encryption Standard to encrypt content in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Secure email and similar messages need a way to scramble the content. This memo says how to use a modern scrambling method called AES in that format.

questions: how does cms encrypt content with aes
which aes key sizes does cms support
subtitle: How to use AES to encrypt message content in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, including how the content key is wrapped for recipients.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needed agreed conventions for using the newer AES cipher as its content encryption algorithm, replacing the older DES.
tldr.mechanism: AES in CBC mode encrypts the content under a random content-encryption key, and that key is wrapped for each recipient by RSA key transport, Diffie-Hellman key agreement, a previously shared key or a password-derived key.
tldr.outcome: It defines the object identifiers for AES-CBC and AES key wrap with 128, 192 and 256-bit keys, and the S/MIME capability encodings that let clients announce AES support.

today: RFC 3565 is a Proposed Standard from July 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Overview and the AES Algorithm
sections.content:
RFC 3565 sets the conventions for using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) as the content encryption algorithm in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), for both the enveloped-data and encrypted-data content types. CMS values are generated using ASN.1 with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).

AES was developed to replace DES. The RFC notes that NIST selected the Rijndael algorithm for its mix of security, performance, efficiency, ease of implementation and flexibility. AES specifies three key sizes: 128, 192 and 256 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: AES is a modern, strong way to scramble data, and it comes with three lock sizes: small, medium and large. This memo says how to use it inside a standard message format.

sections.title: Enveloped-data and Key Management
sections.content:
An enveloped-data message holds encrypted content plus a wrapped copy of the content-encryption key (CEK) for each recipient. The AES CEK MUST be randomly generated for each enveloped-data instance. Implementations MUST support content encryption with AES and MAY support other algorithms.

Four key management techniques can be used to protect the CEK:

  • Key transport: the CEK is encrypted with the recipient's RSA public key. The certificate MUST contain an RSA key, and the key transport algorithm is RSAES-OAEP.
  • Key agreement: a pairwise key-encryption key (KEK) is derived with ephemeral-static or static-static Diffie-Hellman.
  • Previously distributed symmetric KEK: for example a Mail List Key. How it is distributed is out of scope.
  • Password encryption: the KEK is derived from a password or other shared secret.

For key transport, the KeyTransRecipientInfo version MUST be 0 when the recipient is identified by issuer and serial number, and 2 when it is identified by subject key identifier. For key agreement the KeyAgreeRecipient version MUST be 3, and the key encryption algorithm MUST be id-alg-ESDH.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is locked with one random key. Then that key is tucked into a separate envelope for every person who should read it, and each envelope is sealed in a way only that person can open.

sections.title: Wrapping the Content Key with AES
sections.content:
For key agreement, KEK-based and password-based recipients, the CEK is wrapped using the AES key wrap algorithm, which encrypts one AES key in another AES key. The output is 64 bits longer than the input CEK, and the extra bits act as a checksum. The algorithm uses 6*n AES operations, where n is the number of 64-bit blocks in the CEK. Full details are in RFC 3394.

The wrap algorithms are identified by id-aes128-wrap, id-aes192-wrap and id-aes256-wrap, and their parameters field MUST be absent. The identifier gives the KEK size, not the CEK size. Implementations MUST support a KEK and CEK of the same length. If different lengths are supported, the KEK MUST be at least as long as the CEK.

For Diffie-Hellman key agreement, the AES KEK is generated with the method in RFC 2631. The RFC works through two examples that feed a shared secret and the wrap algorithm OID through SHA-1 to produce the key material.
sections.plainLanguage: Key wrap is like putting a small key inside a locked pouch using another key. The pouch's lock must be at least as strong as the key inside, or a thief would just pick the weaker lock.

sections.title: Encrypted-data and Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
The encrypted-data content type carries encrypted content with implicit key management, so there are no recipient structures. Implementations MUST support encryption using AES here too, and the unprotectedAttrs field MAY be present.

AES content encryption uses Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode and is identified by id-aes128-CBC, id-aes192-CBC and id-aes256-CBC. The algorithm parameters field MUST be present and MUST contain an AES-IV, defined as OCTET STRING (SIZE(16)). The identifier goes in the contentEncryptionAlgorithm field of the encrypted content info.
sections.plainLanguage: When both sides already share a key, no envelopes are needed. The message just says which lock size it used and includes a 16-byte starting scramble number.

sections.title: S/MIME Capability Announcements
sections.content:
An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the cryptographic functions it supports with the SMIMECapabilities signed attribute, which MUST be signed by the client. The algorithm identifiers SHOULD be grouped by function and MUST be listed in order of preference.

A client that must support AES symmetric encryption MUST include the AES object identifier among its symmetric algorithms, with the parameter absent. The RFC gives an encoding for each key size. If users require AES, the clients on both the sending and receiving side MUST support it, and it MUST be set in the user preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail programs can tell each other which scrambling methods they know, in order of favourite. That way a sender can pick one the receiver understands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If RSA-OAEP and RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 are both used to transport the same CEK, an attacker can still use the Bleichenbacher attack against the PKCS #1 v1.5 encrypted key, so mixing both in one set of recipients is generally unadvisable.

Implementations must protect the RSA private key and the CEK, since compromise of either can expose messages. AES keys rely on random numbers, and a weak pseudo-random generator can leave little or no security, so the RFC points to RFC 1750 for guidance. When wrapping a CEK, the KEK MUST be at least as long as the CEK, because an attacker works at the weakest point.
sections.plainLanguage: A strong lock does not help if the key is easy to guess, if you leave the key lying around, or if you protect it with a weaker lock than the thing inside.
